power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

info.title: Metacognitive Monitoring in Naturalistic Translation: a Signal Detection Approach

text.text: This study is a secondary analysis of publicly available data from the Center for Research and Innovation in Translation and Translation Technology (CRITT) Translation Process Research Database (TPR-DB; Carl et al., 2016), hosted by CRITT at Kent State University.

The two corpora analysed, BML12 (Carl & Hill, 2012) and SG12 (Carl et al., 2015; Nitzke, 2019), were collected by their original investigators, and ethical oversight of that data collection, including participant consent, rested with those investigators and their institutions.
text.formatted: The two corpora analysed, BML12 <ref type="bibr" target="#b14">(Carl & Hill, 2012)</ref> and SG12 <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Carl et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Nitzke, 2019)</ref>, were collected by their original investigators, and ethical oversight of that data collection, including participant consent, rested with those investigators and their institutions.

text.text: No new data were collected, and no additional ethical approval was sought.
Metacognition describes cognition directed at one's own cognitive processes, and involves the ability to evaluate perceptual states, memories, or decisions (Flavell, 1979; Fleming, 2017).
text.formatted: Metacognition describes cognition directed at one's own cognitive processes, and involves the ability to evaluate perceptual states, memories, or decisions <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Flavell, 1979;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Fleming, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Metacognition includes both monitoring processes, which track information about the state of a cognitive process, and control processes, which use that information to regulate behaviour.
Metacognitive control allows for seeking relevant information, correcting errors and choosing a strategy.
Metacognitive knowledge concerns beliefs about learning, strategies, and conditions a!
ecting performance, while metacognitive skill concerns monitoring confidence and applying an appropriate strategy (Dutemple et al., 2024).
text.formatted: ecting performance, while metacognitive skill concerns monitoring confidence and applying an appropriate strategy <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Dutemple et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In the context of decision-making during perceptual tasks, metacognitive judgements constitute confidence about decisions.
Importantly levels of confidence alone do not correspond with metacognitive ability.

Rather, metacognitive sensitivity refers to the extent to which confidence discriminates between correct and incorrect decisions (Fleming & Lau, 2014), and reflects the precision of underlying internal representations on which decisions are based (Fleming & Daw, 2017).
text.formatted: Rather, metacognitive sensitivity refers to the extent to which confidence discriminates between correct and incorrect decisions <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Fleming & Lau, 2014)</ref>, and reflects the precision of underlying internal representations on which decisions are based <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Fleming & Daw, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Confidence can incorporate evidence supporting a choice, information accumulated after commitment, prior expectations, and beliefs about the decision-making system itself.
For this process to be truly metacognitive, second order judgements formed on first order responses must be based on a meta-level representation of the object-level decision (Fleming, 2024).
text.formatted: For this process to be truly metacognitive, second order judgements formed on first order responses must be based on a meta-level representation of the object-level decision <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">(Fleming, 2024)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, second order confidence judgements based on stimulus information or object-level representations may not require metacognition and can be attained through 'strength-of-evidence' heuristics.
Such models are called 'direct translation' models (Kepecs & Mainen, 2012; Fleming et al., 2012).
text.formatted: Such models are called 'direct translation' models <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Kepecs & Mainen, 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">Fleming et al., 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Alternatively, when additional processing occurs after a decision, the model is post-decisional (Fleming et al., 2012; Yeung & Summerfield, 2012).
text.formatted: Alternatively, when additional processing occurs after a decision, the model is post-decisional <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Fleming et al., 2012;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b60">Yeung & Summerfield, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: In the second order or dual-pathway model proposed by Fleming and Daw (2017), decision and confidence are correlated hidden states.
text.formatted: In the second order or dual-pathway model proposed by <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">Fleming and Daw (2017)</ref>, decision and confidence are correlated hidden states.

text.text: In this framework, as direct access to first-order states is unavailable to confidence calculations, performed actions may reveal additional information for self-evaluation through reflection.
Both this model and the post-decisional model could describe a metacognitive process.
Subjective confidence is thought to be computed by the mismatch between top-down expectations and bottom-up sensory signals.
Distinctions are also made between prospective and retrospective metacognitive judgements.

In the same perceptual discrimination paradigm, retrospective judgements were strongly influenced by the speed and accuracy of the preceding decision, whereas prospective predictions were influenced by confidence over a longer preceding time window.
Global confidence levels were correlated across the prospective and retrospective judgements, suggesting a shared contribution of a stable trait-like metacognitive e!
ciency and distinct local information (Fleming et al., 2016).
text.formatted: ciency and distinct local information <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Fleming et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: The Standard psychophysical approach to studying metacognition is Signal Detection Theory (SDT) (Green & Swets, 1966).
text.formatted: The Standard psychophysical approach to studying metacognition is Signal Detection Theory (SDT) <ref type="bibr" target="#b34">(Green & Swets, 1966)</ref>.

text.text: SDT experiments for studying metacognition involve perceptual decisions (Type-1 task) and confidence reports on them (Type-2 task) to derive measures of performance and metacognition.
In visual discrimination paradigms, a Type-1 task usually involves deciding whether a stimulus is present or not.
After this perceptual decision, the participant estimates whether that choice was correct.
Type-2 judgements are therefore retrospective evaluations of the Type-1 decision (Galvin et al., 2003; Massoni et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Type-2 judgements are therefore retrospective evaluations of the Type-1 decision <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">(Galvin et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">Massoni et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: A participant's performance is measured through sensitivity to the stimulus d → and is the standardised distance between the means of the two Type-1 distributions.
Response bias is represented by a decision threshold or criterion, c which determines the amount of evidence needed to give a certain response.
When c is halfway between the means of the two distributions, the participant is unbiased.
Similar Type-2 measures can be obtained to quantify metacognitive abilities where in this case the two distributions represent judgements of incorrect and correct performance of Type-1 tasks.

When the conditional probabilities of confidence given correct or incorrect performance are cumulated and plotted as a Receiving Operator Characteristic (ROC) curve, a model-free measure of metacognitive sensitivity can be obtained by calculating the area under the curve (AUROC2).
This measure gives the probability that a randomly selected correct trial receives higher confidence than a randomly selected incorrect trial (Massoni et al., 2014).
text.formatted: This measure gives the probability that a randomly selected correct trial receives higher confidence than a randomly selected incorrect trial <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Massoni et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: This measure avoids equal-variance Gaussian assumptions and is una"ected by a tendency to lean towards one response, giving it advantages over correlational measures when response bias is a concern.

To eliminate the influence of Type-1 sensitivity and criterion on Type-2 sensitivity, a di"erent measure -meta-d → assumes a single type 2 ROC is completely determined by an equal-variance Gaussian SDT model (Maniscalco & Lau, 2012).
text.formatted: To eliminate the influence of Type-1 sensitivity and criterion on Type-2 sensitivity, a di"erent measure -meta-d → assumes a single type 2 ROC is completely determined by an equal-variance Gaussian SDT model <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Maniscalco & Lau, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: Meta-d → gives the value of Type-1 performance that an ideal observer would need to generate the observed Type-2 data.

If meta-d → equals d → , confidence is based on as much evidence as predicted for an SDT-optimal observer; a lower value implies loss of decision-relevant evidence in confidence (Fleming 2017; Maniscalco & Lau, 2012).
text.formatted: If meta-d → equals d → , confidence is based on as much evidence as predicted for an SDT-optimal observer; a lower value implies loss of decision-relevant evidence in confidence <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Fleming 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">Maniscalco & Lau, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: The ratio of meta-d → /d → gives the metacognitive e!
ciency, M-ratio (Maniscalco & Lau, 2012).
text.formatted: ciency, M-ratio <ref type="bibr" target="#b40">(Maniscalco & Lau, 2012</ref>).

text.text: An M-ratio of 1 represents the ideal observer case in which meta-d → equals d → .
An M-ratio of 0.7 means that meta-d → is 70% of d → , meaning 30% of the evidence available to the Type-1 decision was lost when confidence was formed (Fleming & Lau, 2014).
text.formatted: An M-ratio of 0.7 means that meta-d → is 70% of d → , meaning 30% of the evidence available to the Type-1 decision was lost when confidence was formed <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">(Fleming & Lau, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: AUROC2 values are bounded between 0.5 and 1.00 for chance to perfect discrimination.
Another SDT-derived measure, m-distance measures propensity to report high or low confidence independent of decision bias and task performance (Sherman et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Another SDT-derived measure, m-distance measures propensity to report high or low confidence independent of decision bias and task performance <ref type="bibr" target="#b52">(Sherman et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Expected values of meta-d → or AUROC2 can vary across studies and depend on factors including task design, sample, and model assumptions.
In one perceptual-confidence experiment involving a dot-comparison task (Massoni et al., 2014) mean AUROC2 was approximately .67 to .66 across subtasks.
text.formatted: In one perceptual-confidence experiment involving a dot-comparison task <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Massoni et al., 2014)</ref> mean AUROC2 was approximately .67 to .66 across subtasks.

text.text: In another graded-confidence visual experiment, age di"erences in AUROC2 were found where values ranged from 0.74 for 5-6 year-olds to 0.79 for adults in one task and 0.73 (age 5-6) to 0.75 (adults) in another task (Watanabe et al., 2025).
text.formatted: In another graded-confidence visual experiment, age di"erences in AUROC2 were found where values ranged from 0.74 for 5-6 year-olds to 0.79 for adults in one task and 0.73 (age 5-6) to 0.75 (adults) in another task <ref type="bibr" target="#b57">(Watanabe et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: An explicit Type-2 judgement involves an expressed evaluation of one's own performance (typically a confidence rating).
On the other hand, implicit measures do not require a direct confidence report.
Examples include response time, opting-out decisions, options to request additional information, and post-decision wagering (Dutemple et al., 2024; Fleming & Lau, 2014).
text.formatted: Examples include response time, opting-out decisions, options to request additional information, and post-decision wagering <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Dutemple et al., 2024;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Fleming & Lau, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: In a preschool visual-identification experiment, explicit confidence reports and implicit clue requests were both positively correlated to each other and school readiness (based on literacy, numeracy, and visual perception). (Dutemple et al., 2024).
text.formatted: In a preschool visual-identification experiment, explicit confidence reports and implicit clue requests were both positively correlated to each other and school readiness (based on literacy, numeracy, and visual perception). <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Dutemple et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: Other work has shown that children seek further information (Call & Carpenter, 2001) or opt out (Balcomb & Gerken, 2008) more when uncertain.
text.formatted: Other work has shown that children seek further information <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Call & Carpenter, 2001)</ref> or opt out <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">(Balcomb & Gerken, 2008)</ref> more when uncertain.

text.text: However, both measures may not be formed of the same internal information: A study comparing explicit confidence reports with implicit wagers found that patients with frontoinsular stroke (FIS) and behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) showed impaired wagering but accurate confidence reports, whereas Alzheimer's disease patients were more likely to su"er impairment in both (García-Cordero et al., 2019).
text.formatted: However, both measures may not be formed of the same internal information: A study comparing explicit confidence reports with implicit wagers found that patients with frontoinsular stroke (FIS) and behavioural variant frontotemporal dementia (bvFTD) showed impaired wagering but accurate confidence reports, whereas Alzheimer's disease patients were more likely to su"er impairment in both <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(García-Cordero et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Explicit and implicit measures may therefore distinguish inaccurate self-evaluation from failure to use available evaluative information to control action.

Moreover, Nicholson and colleagues (2021) suggest that explicit metacognitive tasks involving reflection and verbal reports on internal states draw on metarepresentational resources, whereas implicit task gambles may not require this, corresponding with first order models of metacognition (Fleming & Daw, 2017).
text.formatted: Moreover, <ref type="bibr">Nicholson and colleagues (2021)</ref> suggest that explicit metacognitive tasks involving reflection and verbal reports on internal states draw on metarepresentational resources, whereas implicit task gambles may not require this, corresponding with first order models of metacognition <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Fleming & Daw, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: In one post-decision wagering task, (Moreira et al., 2018) certainty readouts about being incorrect were associated with meta-d → exceeding d → , meaning confidence discriminated correct from incorrect decisions better than accuracy alone would allow, suggesting that confidence computation draws on information beyond the decision variable itself.
text.formatted: In one post-decision wagering task, <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Moreira et al., 2018</ref>) certainty readouts about being incorrect were associated with meta-d → exceeding d → , meaning confidence discriminated correct from incorrect decisions better than accuracy alone would allow, suggesting that confidence computation draws on information beyond the decision variable itself.

text.text: Other implicit indicators, such as response time, information seeking and clue selection, must first be translated to ordinal second-order choices based on object-level accuracy to obtain measures of metacognitive sensitivity.
A standard metacognitive SDT experiment involves independent trials consisting of a Type-1 and Type-2 tasks with the objective of disentangling confidence bias, sensitivity and e!
ciency.
Most everyday tasks involving metacognition involve decisions and confidence as processes that unfold over time as evidence accumulates.
Evidence accumulation models have described confidence as the di"erence between maximal evidence and a decision bound (Pereira et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Evidence accumulation models have described confidence as the di"erence between maximal evidence and a decision bound <ref type="bibr" target="#b48">(Pereira et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Drift-di"usion simulations and binary perceptual task data show that M-ratio changes with response caution, both with and without instructions to prioritise speed or accuracy.
A proposed dynamic measure, v-ratio, did not show this speed-accuracy e"ect (Desender et al., 2022).
text.formatted: A proposed dynamic measure, v-ratio, did not show this speed-accuracy e"ect <ref type="bibr" target="#b21">(Desender et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: The process of human translation, being inherently metalinguistic and context-dependent makes it a valuable domain for studying metacognition: translators assess implicit and explicit knowledge about semantics, syntax, context-derived relevance and make cross-linguistic judgements about semantic content, genre, register, and usage (Halverson, 2018) in order to make production decisions.
text.formatted: The process of human translation, being inherently metalinguistic and context-dependent makes it a valuable domain for studying metacognition: translators assess implicit and explicit knowledge about semantics, syntax, context-derived relevance and make cross-linguistic judgements about semantic content, genre, register, and usage <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Halverson, 2018)</ref> in order to make production decisions.

text.text: In the monitor model (Tirkkonen-Condit, 2005; Carl & Dragsted, 2012) translation is initially guided by automated routines, while monitoring becomes more prominent when the target text presents a challenge.
text.formatted: In the monitor model <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Tirkkonen-Condit, 2005;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Carl & Dragsted, 2012)</ref> translation is initially guided by automated routines, while monitoring becomes more prominent when the target text presents a challenge.

text.text: Bursts of production, pauses, gaze patterns, edits, and revision behaviour can be tracked with keystroke and eye-tracking data, along with timestamps, allowing for mappings between observed reading and typing behaviour and source and target text token positions (Carl, 2009; Carl & Jakobsen, 2009) This data does not give direct access to internal cognitive processes but temporal resolution means that monitoring can be examined as a process that unfolds with time through the gradual knowledge accumulation of a source text.

text.text: Translation Process Research (TPR) currently uses mixed-method approaches such as qualitative meta-analysis (Xie & Wang, 2025) annotated translation (Costa & da Silva, 2023) and triangulation (Alves, 2003). for studying metacognition. Xie and Wang (2025) conducted a meta-analysis on 23 studies finding a positive association between metacognition and translation competence.

text.text: However, this study aggregated existing measures, including questionnaire and interview-based measures, rather than measures of metacognitive sensitivity or e!
ciency.

Alves, (2005) presents a framework where meta-reflection bridges procedural skill (automatized translation performance) and declarative and explanatory articulation (knowing what and why translation decisions were made) by allowing procedural knowledge to become increasingly consciously accessible to the translator as expertise increases.
However, this framework provides no quantitative measure of metareflection.

Furthermore, Costa & da Silva (2023) argue for concomitant annotation during translation as a pedagogical approach instead of retrospective annotation as the latter does not require the monitoring processes that occur during translation.
text.formatted: Furthermore, <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Costa & da Silva (2023)</ref> argue for concomitant annotation during translation as a pedagogical approach instead of retrospective annotation as the latter does not require the monitoring processes that occur during translation.

text.text: They mention that empirical evidence is needed to support this claim. Halverson (2018) expresses the need for sharper distinctions between metalinguistic knowledge, awareness, and ability, speculating that metalinguistic knowledge precedes awareness and ability. Gutt (2004) suggests that metarepresentational ability is an important aspect of translation competence as it involves managing mismatches between di"erent cognitive environments (Sperber & Wilson, 1995) and audiences.

text.text: In line with the domain-general nature of metacognition, Whyatt and Naranowicz (2020) suggest that planning, self-monitoring, and self-revision can transfer from translation to intralingual paraphrasing once a threshold level of expertise has been reached. Pinet and Nozari (2020), applied a signal detection framework to error correction in typing.

text.text: In a single-word typing-to-dictation task, participants heard a word and typed it under a time limit.
An error was defined objectively, as a keystroke sequence that di"ered from the intended word.
Monitoring was identified based on whether the typist attempted a correction, (pressing the backspace key), and an explicit report on whether the participant believed they had made an error.
They found systematic evidence of correction attempts that were not explicitly reported.
They explain such repairs as largely automatic and occurring without attentional control.

Translation styles are distinct, relatively stable procedural patterns in how translators allocate attention through reading and producing text, drafting a target text, pausing between production, and making revisions.

Translation progression graphs integrate fixations on source and target tokens with keystroke data across a duration of time. Carl et al. (2011) have identified distinct styles of orientation, drafting and revision.
text.formatted: Translation progression graphs integrate fixations on source and target tokens with keystroke data across a duration of time. <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Carl et al. (2011)</ref> have identified distinct styles of orientation, drafting and revision.

text.text: For example, head-starters begin translation immediately whereas large-context-planners read far ahead into the source text before beginning production.
Similarly, Chen et al. (2025) used clustering to identify three distinct preparatory-reading patterns: Fast Surface-level, Systematic Deep-level, and Extended Iterative.
text.formatted: Similarly, <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">Chen et al. (2025)</ref> used clustering to identify three distinct preparatory-reading patterns: Fast Surface-level, Systematic Deep-level, and Extended Iterative.

text.text: A standardised, quantitative measure of metacognitive sensitivity during translation has not yet been demonstrated for translation.

This paper addresses this by applying SDT to translation process data from multiple translators and translation sessions from the Translation Process Research Database (TPR-DB) and calculates AUROC2 values for individual translators across 2 language pairs.
The present study is organised as follows.

Section 2 explicates the methodology, introducing, the two TPR-DB corpora (BML12, English-Spanish; SG12, English-German), how production units are assembled into trials where a Type-1 decision is paired with a Type-2 response, how initial productions are scored against each participant's final translation.
It also explains the implicit behavioural proxy used for the Type-2 response under a lower and an upper bound for defining a response window before AUROC2 is defined.
Section 3 reports the results at the aggregate and participant levels under both regimes, together with robustness checks.
Section 4 discusses the implications for metacognitive monitoring in naturalistic translation, the main limitations, and directions for future work.
This analysis draws on two studies from the TPR-DB (Carl et al., 2016).
text.formatted: This analysis draws on two studies from the TPR-DB <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Carl et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Data acquisition software Translog-II was used to record keystrokes with timestamps to the millisecond, insertions and deletions, and cursor o"set.
Gaze data was recorded via a Tobii T120 eye tracker with tracking fixations and timestamps on a source or target window.

Post-hoc alignment (Carl, 2009; Carl & Jakobsen, 2009) between keystrokes, fixations and source and target tokens, as well as temporal and positional information are accessible through tables in the TPR-DB allowing for detection and analysis of behavioural events without access to the original recordings (Carl, 2012).

text.text: The study used 2 corpora which were part of the TPR-DB MultiLingual series: BML12, an English-to-Spanish study (Carl & Hill, 2012), and SG12, an English-to-German study (Carl et al., 2015; Nitzke, 2019).

text.text: Both use a common set of six English source texts (110-160 words per text -four obtained from news sources and two from a sociological encyclopaedia with 847 words in total) which were translated into several target languages under a shared experimental design.
Although both corpora contain recordings of several task types, only from-scratch translation sessions (of the form P20 T4) were used in this study.
Each session involves only one participant and there were no time limits placed on translation sessions.
The two studies were selected on three grounds: 1.
Shared materials, recording apparatus and experimental design to control for text di!
culty, measurement and task structure.
Same source language so that di"erences in reading behaviour are not a result of di"erences in source-text syntactical structure.
Typologically distinct target languages so that cross-linguistic replication can be scrutinised.
Overview of corpora: BML12: Consists of 32 participants and 60 sessions, 9,938 target tokens, 411 target segments and 10.34 hours of production.
Each translation session was approximately 20 minutes long, with some running up to over an hour.
Participants were a mixture of students and experienced translators, but the exact split is unknown (Carl & Hill, 2012; Carl & Schae"er, 2017). 28 of 32 participants contributed 2 sessions each.

text.text: Translation sessions are algorithmically divided into three phases (Jakobsen, 2002; Carl et al., 2011): Orientation, where source text is initially read, Drafting, where the target text is initially produced, and Revision, where the produced text is reviewed and amended.

text.text: Phases are included in session tables in TPR-DB.
By definition, no keystrokes occur during Orientation and Drafting is identified by the sequentiality of successive keystrokes and is required to account for at least half of a session's keystrokes.
Its endpoint is based on the production of the last word of the target text rather than the translation of the last source word.
The remaining Revision phase typically involves both insertions and deletions.
A SDT experimental paradigm must include a decision (Type-1), involving a binary choice and a response (Type-2) consisting of a confidence report.
Each trial is formed of one Type-1 task and its corresponding Type-2 task.

The TPR-DB contains unit tables that aggregate keystrokes and fixations into behaviourally interpretable segments (Carl, 2014; Carl et al., 2016) such as activity units (AU -6 types based on whether reading and/or typing occurred and whether reading occurred on the source or target text) and translation units (TU -formed by combining a stretch of production with the immediately preceding fixations).

text.text: This study uses production units (PU): bursts of typing, separated by pauses (production unit breaks -PUB).

A PUB is a pause whose duration is treated as reflective rather than automated processing, and is located wherever an inter-keystroke interval (IKI -the pause between a non-alphanumerical keystroke and a successive alphanumerical keystroke) exceeds a text-specific quantile threshold on the IKI distribution.

Following Bandaru, Carl & Ren (2026), the threshold is set at the quantile 1/(c → k), where c is the average characters per word for a given text and k the chunk length in number of words (language based) (with c ↑ 6 and k = 3 for English placing it at 5.5% of IKIs), A similar measure (Muñoz Martín & Apfelthaler, 2022), the 'Task Segment Pause' (TSP) is a pause exceeding a threshold of 3↓ median between-word inter-keystroke interval.

This study used only keystroke data and PUs as the foundational task units.
Each PU is the basis for either a Type-1 decision or Type-2 response.
Trials constructed as such are not independent in the sense assumed by classical signal detection theory because adjacent spans of source text are semantically correlated.
This dependence is impossible to eliminate when applying SDT to a complex, naturalistic, continuous cognitive task without interruption.
However, using PUs as task units provides adequate mitigation and they are selected as base units for the following reasons: 1.
PUs are delimited by pauses thought to indicate cognition on the span of text they surround (TPR-DB fixation tables).
This allows for a time gap between tasks within a trial so that decision and response are separated.
PUs are small, cognitive units corresponding to deliberate decisions the translator makes.
Recorded information in the TPR-DB tables gives us access to exactly what was typed and deleted within a PU, and the target-token identifiers map production to the final target text.
PUs are not fixed-time units and vary in length and di!
culty.
However, as the source texts are of similar di!
culty, participant-level behaviour is largely una"ected by individual PU di"erences within the large number of PUs in each session.
Each trial consists of:
A Type-1 decision: A PU containing an initial target production which is either correct (1) or incorrect (0), based on perception of the corresponding source text as the stimulus.
Correctness of the initial production is measured against the corresponding text in the final translation post-revision (discussed ahead).
A Type-2 response: A subsequent decision where it is decided whether or not reformulation is needed.

Type-2 task = 2 (high confidence) if no reformulation occurs during drafting and Type-2 task = 1 (low confidence) if reformulation of an already produced span of text occurs in a later PU during Drafting.
The PU where reformulation occurs can be anywhere between (and including) the PUB immediately following the corresponding Type-1 PU and the final PU of the drafting phase within a session.
This range supplies the lower and upper bounds of the response window.
Pairing was performed strictly within participant and session, so the final unit of one session was never paired with the first unit of another.
Response units do not overlap with decision units; a Type-1 trial records a span of target text the translator committed to initially.
Subsequent behaviour, on which a Type-2 task response is derived, either lets it stand or reformulates it.
Neither study collected confidence ratings; participants translated without interruption.
The Type-2 response is therefore an implicit proxy measure, inferred from the available behavioural data.

Importantly, a Type-2 task labelled as a reformulation need not reformulate the entire span of text produced during the initial PU but it must be a correction of at least 1 word from the initial span that amounts to more than correcting a motor slip (discussed further).
This framework assumes that not reformulating a Type-1 production during Drafting means the translator chose not to reformulate that span because they considered it unnecessary.
This allows for the translation process to proceed in a naturalistic way.

Despite the 'incorrect' and 'correct' Type-1 labels, reformulation may replace a span of text because a better formulation became available regardless of whether the initial production was objectively incorrect.
Such trials are still coded as Type-1 task = 0.

Furthermore, all PUs were drawn from the Drafting phase because an initial production choice is, by definition, made during the first production, and a reformulation signals monitoring only if it is made while that production is still current.

On the other hand, changes made during Revision are the product of systematic later review: this phase does not reflect a purely metacognitive process since the translator reads their produced target text to verify its accuracy rather than reflecting on their own past behaviour from when the span of text was initially produced.
All Revision-phase PUs are excluded from analysis accordingly.
Excluding Revision-phase PUs does not preclude the e"ect of Revision on the final text.
A Type-1 task is correct if it survived in its recognisable form, into the participant's own final translation.

A production that the translator leaves alone during Drafting but later replaces during Revision is recorded as incorrect (at the time of the trial) because the translator only caught the problem later on in review.

Stated clearly, Since we assume that each translator has a working knowledge of the language, 'Revision' is treated as a phase during which, all trials are complete and Type-1 accuracy is evaluated based on the translators' own judgement.
The use of the final text as the criterion is justified because: 1.
It provides a translator-calibrated measure of accuracy.
Unlike the standard signal detection approach, translation, a complex and partly subjective task, admits no external ground truth of comparable status: a rendering may be more or less appropriate.

Whether a participant's evaluation at the moment of initial production anticipates their own later, considered judgement is the metacognitive question being investigated in this study by keeping both the Type-1 outcome and the Type-2 judgement within a single participant's frame of reference.

External verification would measure whether confidence tracks someone else's standard of accuracy, which conflates metacognitive sensitivity with whether the translator and verifier share the same notion of "correct".
The final translation, can be regarded as 'correct' provided all 'errors' were detected during Revision.

Since there was no time limit placed on producing the final translation (Nitzke, 2019; Carl & Hill, 2012), we take the final translation as what the translator deemed as correct and most appropriate, based on the assumption that the participant picks up on all Drafting 'errors'.

text.text: Since both Type-1 and 2 task definitions involve whether a span of text was changed, AUROC2 values can only be viewed as useful or accurate if the following assumptions hold enough to eliminate the confound between Type-1 and 2: 1.
A semantically substantive drafting reformulation reflects a deliberate monitoring decision concerning the corresponding initial production.

Revision is assumed to identify and retain a suitably acceptable translation, such that the final translation provides the criterion against which the validity of the initial production can be evaluated.
When translators detect that an initial production is incorrect, they prefer to replace it with a correct formulation during Drafting rather than deferring the correction to Revision.
These three assumptions are consistent with the structure of the task and with previous research in the field.
Assumption 1 is supported by the method used to assign Type-2 reformulations (Section 2.3).
This approach is not infallible but it is designed to exclude motor slips so that reformulations are the product of a more evaluative act.
Assumption 2 is supported by the participant pool and experimental design: both student and professional translators were of su!
cient competence and sessions were not constrained by a time limit.
Consequently, final translations can be expected to represent considered renderings and the translators' final judgement.
Assumption 3 is what allows Drafting reformulation to serve as the locus of online monitoring.
According to the Monitor Model, problematic renderings are addressed as they arise (Tirkkonen-Condit, 2005).
text.formatted: According to the Monitor Model, problematic renderings are addressed as they arise <ref type="bibr" target="#b55">(Tirkkonen-Condit, 2005)</ref>.

text.text: This could be explained by the demands of working memory: a detected problem that is left unresolved incurs an additional cognitive load that must be carried for as long as production continues without making the correction (Levelt, 1983).

text.text: However, the Type-1/Type-2 confound cannot be entirely eliminated within a self-defined accuracy framework.
AUROC2 remains informative nevertheless; It is computed identically across two distinct language corpora such that the reliability and reproducibility of the results can be scrutinised.
Task 1: In CRITT edit notation, a bracketed span records deleted characters, so hoka[ak]la resolves to hola.

To assess task 1 accuracy, the typed text in each PU was recovered and compared against the span of the final target text at the same token positions, using a partialratio 'fuzzy match' scaled from 0 to 100.
PUs scoring at or above 75 were coded Type-1 = 1 (correct); those below were coded Type-1 = 0.

The value of 75 was chosen to permit orthographic variation and the propagation of neighbouring edits into a span's boundary, while excluding cases where the final span is a substantively di"erent rendering.
Two considerations support this: 1.
The fuzzy score is a noisy index of the latent binary state, discriminating between correct and incorrect production.
A superficial change such as an added accent, or a shifted clitic due to a neighbouring edit should still code as correct.
A sparse region exists around the chosen value.

Task 2: To detect reformulations and distinguish typing noise due to motor slips from evaluative judgements, a trial was coded Type-2 task = 1 (low confidence) only if three conditions held jointly: 1. the PU was of 'Type' Deletion or Combined (deletion and insertion) -it removed material rather than only appending.
The PU target tokens overlapped the corresponding Type-1 target tokens.

The deleted material satisfied a content condition, distinguishing reformulation from motor slips: A deletion is reformulation if it contains at least two letters and crosses a word boundary, or at least five letters within a single word.
The third condition captures withdrawals of formulation while largely excluding the repair of slips and was evaluated over the bracketed deletion spans of the edit string.
Letters were counted with a Unicode-aware pattern treating accented characters as letters and excluding digits, punctuation and the underscore used to mark spaces.
A deletion under these constraints, implies the removal of material spanning a word boundary or that a word was rewritten rather than repaired.

text.text: To admit an appropriate time span for the Type-2 judgement, both a lower and an upper bound are reported for the same quantity.
Lower bound: Type-2 = 1 is assigned only if the immediately following production unit reformulates the preceding unit's tokens.
This is the strictest reading of online monitoring where detection and action are contiguous.
This necessarily underestimates sensitivity.
Upper bound: Type-2 = 1 is assigned if any subsequent production unit within the drafting phase reformulates the preceding unit's tokens.
This admits deferred action while maintaining the requirement that the reformulation occurs during the Drafting phase.

The two bounds are informative in di"erent ways: The lower bound characterises immediately expressed monitoring (occurs after just a PUB); the upper bound characterises monitoring that manifests at any point within the same Drafting episode.
The problem could be detected immediately after the Type-1 task or at any point before the reformulation is made.
A larger distance between the upper and lower bound could identify a translator who registers a problem but defers acting on it or registers it later.
Conversely, a small gap implies a case where detection occurs early and is more tightly coupled with action.
Because the upper bound admits a larger set of reformulation events within drafting, it gives a more complete estimate of metacognitive sensitivity, while the lower bound serves as a floor.
Metacognitive sensitivity is quantified as the area under the Type-2 receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC2; Galvin et al., 2003; Fleming & Lau, 2014).
text.formatted: Metacognitive sensitivity is quantified as the area under the Type-2 receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC2; <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Galvin et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Fleming & Lau, 2014)</ref>.

text.text: With a binary confidence report, the Type-2 ROC has a single empirical operating point and the area under the curve is: where H2 = P (Type-2 = 2 | Type-1 = 1) is the proportion of correct productions left unreformulated in Drafting and F2 = P (Type-2 = 2 | Type-1 = 0) is the proportion of incorrect productions left unreformulated in Drafting (false-alarm).
Under this convention, high confidence is expressed by leaving a production unreformulated, while low confidence is expressed as a reformulation decision.
AUROC2 = 0.5 implies chance discrimination, suggesting that reformulation behaviour during Drafting is independent of production accuracy.
Values above 0.5 indicate that the decision to return and reformulate discriminates the translator's own correct from their own incorrect productions.
Read as a ranking statistic, AUROC2 gives the probability that a randomly chosen incorrect production receives lower implicit confidence than a randomly chosen correct production.

The four possible trial cases existing under this design are: (unreformulated | correct): the translator leaves an initially correct production alone during Drafting (characterised as a 'hit') (unreformulated | incorrect): the translator does not reformulate a production that is later deemed incorrect during Revision (false alarm).
(reformulated | correct): a correct production is reformulated during Drafting but the translator later reverts to the initial choice during Revision.
(reformulated | incorrect): the translator catches an incorrect production and reformulates during Drafting.

text.text: Across corpora, correct productions account for 77-78% of trials, and unreformulated trials account for 94% under the lower bound and 82-86% under the upper bound.

Of the 4 possible combinations, reformulated incorrect productions form the smallest group, containing 74 trials in SG12, and reformulated correct productions form the smallest group (containing 85 trials) in BML12, under the lower bound.
Meta-d → requires fitting an equal-variance Gaussian model to the contingency table by maximum-likelihood.
With unbalanced populations, parametric extrapolation depends heavily on the sparse case.
AUROC2 is computed directly from the observed conditional proportions and involves no such extrapolation (Fleming and Lau, 2014).

Under both bounds sparsity is substantial: under the lower bound 21 of 32 BML12 participants and 19 of 24 SG12 participants have fewer than five trials in the incorrect-and-reformulated cell.
Under the upper bound this is ten and nine respectively.
All quantities are computed within participant and then aggregated across participants so the translator is the standard unit of statistical inference.
Group-level intervals are obtained by resampling participants rather than trials, preserving existing dependence within each participant's data.
Estimates should therefore, be read as characterising individual translators.
The Drafting phase accounts for approximately nine tenths of PUs in both corpora, suggesting most productive activity occurred during Drafting.
The trials analysed here are drawn exclusively from this phase and capture the majority of each participant's production. the Revision phase, by contrast, contributes a small minority of units.
Per-participant median Drafting proportions were 0.91 for BML12 (range 0.45-1.00) and 0.96 for SG12 (range 0.67-0.99).

Under the lower bound, 6.2% of gradable initial productions in BML12 and 6.3% in SG12 were followed immediately by a reformulation of the same span of text.
Under the upper bound, this rises to 14.2% and 17.8% respectively.

The upper bound therefore includes 2.3 times as many reformulation events as the lower bound in BML12 and 2.8 times as many in SG12; most reformulation during Drafting is deferred to later in the Drafting phase rather than immediate.
The two corpora largely correspond on the absolute rates and the multiplier.
Under the upper bound, 66.4% of incorrect productions in BML12 and 57.0% in SG12 were not reformulated at any point during Drafting.

These are categorised as false alarms (under the convention used, high confidence in a production that was in fact incorrect is a false alarm) that were only corrected during Revision or displaced by later restructuring.

text.text: The di"erence in values between bounds is considerable: admitting monitoring from initial production across the whole response window increases the deviation from chance by 76% in BML12 (from 0.067 to 0.118 above chance) and by 224% in SG12 (from 0.039 to 0.125), with absolute increases of 0.051 and 0.086.
The large relative change suggests that the lower bound is substantially conservative.
Pooled across all 56 participants, sensitivity is bracketed between 0.555 and 0.621.

text.text: The two corpora converge under the upper bound.
At the lower bound the group means di"er by 0.028 (0.567 and 0.539); at the upper bound the di"erence is 0.007 (0.618 and 0.625), with substantially overlapping intervals.
Metacognitive monitoring in naturalistic translation is therefore, detectable and the strength of evidence rests on e"ect size, narrowness of intervals and convergence across independent corpora.
When the response window is widened, group estimates di"er by less than the width of either interval.
This provides evidence that the measure captures a reliable signal rather than a feature of one dataset.
The discrepancy between corpora at the lower bound can be attributed to a di"erence in the temporal distribution of reformulations.
The German cohort deferred a larger proportion of their reformulations to later in the drafting phase.
Once deferred reformulations are admitted, this di"erence becomes minor.

The asymmetry is visible in the conditional probabilities: the proportion of incorrect productions left unreformulated falls from 86.6% to 57.0% in SG12 between bounds against 83.4% to 66.4% in BML12.
SG12 deferred far more of its error-reformulations to later in drafting.
SG12's longer PUBs (median 3,604 vs 1,891 ms) o"er one plausible explanation for this di"erence: they might process spans of text in larger chunks.
However, whether German syntactic structure delays the point at which a problem becomes apparent cannot be determined from this data and remains a question for item-level analysis.

text.text: At or above-chance sensitivity is near-universal in both cohorts: under the upper bound every participant in SG12 and 31 of 32 in BML12 exceeded chance.
The upper bound raises and disperses the distribution.
The standard deviation increases from 0.043 to 0.071 in BML12 and 0.031 to 0.080 in SG12, and the range widens from 0.173 to 0.338 and 0.120 to 0.297 respectively.
Widening the response window separates the estimates by capturing more signal (as well as sampling variability), revealing variation that the restricted window compressed toward chance.
This is expected as only counting immediate reformulations makes participants who defer reformulation indistinguishable from those who fail to detect inaccuracy.
Therefore, the upper bound can be viewed as a more complete measure of metacognitive sensitivity despite carrying more noise.

text.text: Between-participant variance in AUROC2 is almost entirely driven by F 2 (0.615-1 in BML12 and 0.769-1 in SG12), which varies much more than H 2 , which is near-constant across participants (0.920-1 in BML12 and 0.909-0.978 in SG12).
AUROC2 correlates highly with P(reformulated | incorrect), contributing 91% (SG12) and 95% (BML12) of between participant variance.

However, AUROC2 is still superior to the fraction of total corrections occurring during Drafting; AUROC2 provides more information about whether reformulations are well-targeted by assessing both accuracy and reformulation for each span of produced text and identifies reversions.
This is especially critical for prospective studies using externally evaluated accuracy measures or involving samples with very di"erent reformulation behaviour.
The obtained AUROC2 values can also be used to compare estimates to the wider metacognition literature for tasks unrelated to translation.
Metacognitive sensitivity was not higher among more accurate translators.
Grouping participants into quartiles for each corpus by Type-1 accuracy, per-participant mean AUROC2 was lowest in the top quartile in both corpora under both bounds (see Figure 4).

Excluding it, ω falls to +0.00 and ↔0.15.
The relatively lower sensitivity in the highest accuracy quartile cannot simply be explained by a statistical artifact.

Under the lower bound, in the bottom and top quartiles, F 2 rises from 0.838 to 0.872 in BML12 and from 0.883 to 0.923 in SG12, while H 2 remains essentially unchanged (0.969 to 0.974; 0.950 to 0.956), narrowing the H 2 → F 2 gap; the gap between the two closes due to false alarms rather than the hit rate.
The same pattern holds under the upper bound, where F 2 rises from 0.594 to 0.797 in BML12 and from 0.525 to 0.810 in SG12; H 2 also rises (0.879 to 0.957; 0.832 to 0.913), but by considerably less.
The gap again closes mainly through false alarms.

However, because these translators produce fewer initial errors, F 2 estimates rest on fewer trials per participant (a mean of 14.4 and 11.8 incorrect trials in the top quartile, against 37.5 and 40.7 in the bottom), so individual values should be read as less precise.
Of the 56 participants, 47 (84%) had a higher AUROC2 under the upper bound than the lower.
The mean increase was 0.051 in BML12, where 24 of 32 participants increased, and 0.086 in SG12, where 23 of 24 increased.

Eight of the nine participants whose AUROC2 did not increase showed small decreases and one showed no change, 0.026 being the largest, and seven of the nine were in the upper half of their cohort's accuracy distribution.
For these translators, reformulations made immediately were more diagnostic of inaccuracy than deferred reformulations.
The size of individual gains varied considerably, from ↔0.026 to 0.22.

This variation is a descriptive property contributing to the notion of translation style: a participant whose AUROC2 changes little between bounds is more likely to act promptly on detection, whereas a translator whose estimate rises substantially may defer acting until the remaining, relevant span of text has been produced.
Reporting only one bound would not capture these di"erences.
One BML12 participant (P24) contributed 40 gradable trials of which only two were incorrect and made no reformulations at all under either bound.
Their AUROC2 is returned as exactly 0.500, which reflects the absence of variation rather than a measurement of chance-level sensitivity.
It is the only such case in either corpus and the participant is retained in all reported means.

Excluding them leaves conclusions unchanged: BML12 group AUROC2 becomes 0.569 [0.555, 0.585] under the lower bound and 0.622 [0.599, 0.646] under the upper bound, and the combined estimates across cohorts become 0.556 [0.546, 0.567] and 0.623 [0.605, 0.643].

Restricting the analysis to participants contributing at least 20 incorrect trials, which removes the sparsest contingency tables, also leaves the pattern intact: BML12 (n = 20) gives 0.567 [0.553, 0.583] and 0.618 [0.593, 0.642]; SG12 (n = 12) gives 0.548 [0.530, 0.566] and 0.669 [0.626, 0.713].
The classification of a PU as correct or incorrect depends on a 'fuzzy-match' threshold, fixed at 75 (Section 2.3).
As this is a free parameter, the analysis was repeated at four alternative threshold values.
Type-1 accuracy varies from 0.80 at a threshold of 65 to 0.73 at a threshold of 85, a shift of 228 (BML12) and 172 (SG12) trials between classes across the full range.

As discussed in Section 2.2, under the assumption that revision identifies all correct and incorrect drafting translations, the confound between type-1 and 2 is su!
ciently mitigated: a reformulation can drive a PU to be incorrect, independently of whether that PU was destined for a di"erent rendering post-revision.

Additionally, under a self-assessed accuracy metric, the assumption that a translator will only replace a span of text if they deem another rendering preferable, and that errors detected in Drafting are reformulated in Drafting, the dependence is at most partial: 60.8% of Type-2 = 1 trials in BML12 and 47.7% in SG12 are coded Type-1 = 0 under the lower bound, against roughly 100% were the link entirely mechanical.
Nevertheless, a tipping-point sensitivity analysis was undertaken to establish how large the mechanical component would need to be to wholly account for the result.
Let t denote the proportion of incorrect-reformulated trials that are incorrect solely due to reformulation and that would otherwise have been correct.

Reassigning that fraction to the correct row and recomputing gives AUROC2 as a function of t, with t = 0 the primary analysis and t = 1, the case where no reformulated PU would have been replaced on its own.
The estimate declines smoothly and reaches 0.5 at t = 0.68 in BML12 and t = 0.53 in SG12 under the lower bound, and at t = 0.69 and t = 0.69 under the upper.
Combining the cohorts yields t = 0.63 under the lower bound and t = 0.69 under the upper bound (Figure 5).

text.text: Taking the lower limit of the bootstrap interval rather than the mean moves these values to 0.63, 0.44, 0.64 and 0.61.

In every case but one, more than half of all drafting reformulations that produced an incorrect PU would have to be altering the final text for reasons unconnected to the PUs accuracy before the deviation from chance were eliminated.
The exception is SG12 under the lower bound at t = 0.44.

Moreover, given that the detection of reformulations involves filtering out motor slips, this level of contamination is implausible as surviving Type-2 = 1 events are mostly considered deliberate withdrawals of formulation rather than incidental deletions.
The finding is therefore robust to moderate mechanical contamination and AUROC2 values should be read conservatively as upper limits on metacognitive sensitivity.
Although motor slips are filtered out of reformulations, the filter does not evaluate position.

Under the lower bound, all three Type-2 = 1 conditions (Section 2.3) may be satisfied if a given PU has a following PU where new material is typed and backspaced through its own characters, touching the first PU without altering its production at all.
This means that a trial can be coded as reformulated without actually being altered and 'leaks' into the reformulated category.
Target-token overlap is established by a single shared token at the unit boundary.

Because CRITT notation records a bracketed span as the characters removed, this can be identified directly: a deletion reaches into a preceding PU only where its length exceeds the running total of characters typed within the current PU, and a leak is a deletion that stayed within that unit's own typing.
Deletions landing exactly on the boundary are ambiguous.
Therefore, both a strict and an inclusive criterion are reported, where the strict criterion yields the higher leak estimate.
Between 9.7% (inclusive) and 18.4% (strict) of reformulated PUs in BML12, and between 15.5% (inclusive) and 21.9% (strict) in SG12, are confined to the PU's own typing.

This leak is concentrated among correct-reformulated trials: under the strict criterion, 95.5% of deletions in incorrect-reformulated trials reach the preceding production in BML12 and 89.2% in SG12, compared to only 60.0% and 67.9% in correct-reformulated trials.

Yet recoding the confined cases to Type-2 = 2 leaves AUROC2 almost unchanged: BML12 moves from 0.567 to 0.569 under the strict criterion and remains at 0.567 under the inclusive, and SG12 from 0.539 to 0.539 (strict) and 0.537 (inclusive), because only a small number of trials are recoded (40 and 34 under the strict criterion, 21 and 24 under the inclusive).
The changes are at most 0.002 in either direction.
In conclusion, contamination exists but is close to neutral for the discrimination measure.

The diagnostic cannot be applied to the upper bound, where the reformulating unit may fall several units later and its edit string is not retained in the trial table; the lower-bound result is reported as the conservative case.

This study uses translation as a task to demonstrate a novel SDT design for complex, naturalistic tasks, where confidence can be obtained without probing to allow for uninterrupted task completion and where monitoring may be continuous, allowing for evidence accumulation throughout the task.

This was done by using implicit behavioural proxies as decision (initial production of a span of text being correct or incorrect) and response variables (low or high confidence based on whether or not reformulation occurred during drafting), and the response window was delimited by a lower and upper bound during which a type-2 response can be made.
Trials are not fully independent but are treated as such by using pre-existing behavioural units called production units.
The method was applied on behavioural data collected during previous studies.

AUROC2 was calculated to measure how well Drafting reformulation was able to discriminate between self-assessed correct and incorrect productions, where the type-1 task was the production of a span of text and the type-2 task was 1 or 2 depending on whether or not reformulation of that span of text later took place during the Drafting phase.

The method defined a window during which any reformulation (type-2 response) on any already completed type-1 decision (produced PU) could be made, by defining a window beginning immediately after initial production and ending at the end of the Drafting phase.
AUROC2 was chosen as a more suitable metric than meta-d → due to sparsely distributed conditionals.
The measure used the final translation post-Revision as a self-assessed accuracy metric against which to judge type-1 accuracy.
This choice was made to accurately quantify whether confidence tracks a translator's own standard of accuracy.
Two distinct language corpora were used (English-Spanish, BML12 and English-German, SG12).

The Group AUROC2 was 0.567 and 0.539 under the lower bound, 0.618 and 0.625 under the upper for BML12 and SG12 respectively, with every bootstrap interval excluding 0.5 and P (> 0.5) = 1.000 throughout.

text.text: A small participant range between lower and upper bounds implies more immediate reformulation.
By design, the upper bound captured a larger set of type-2 tasks and thus produced higher AUROC2 estimates.
These higher estimates are expected to be more in line with true metacognitive sensitivity.

Under the upper bound, 33.6% (BML12) and 43.0% (SG12) of eventually-altered productions are reformulated during drafting rather than left to revision; the remainder (66.4% and 57.0%) are false alarms of online monitoring.
Under the lower bound, 16.6% (BML12) and 13.4% (SG12) of eventually-altered productions are reformulated during drafting.

Two typologically distinct language pairs converge, and converge more closely under the more complete measure: the cross-corpus gap narrows from 0.028 to 0.007 when the upper bound replaces the lower.
Sensitivity is broadly distributed rather than concentrated: 31 of 32 and 24 of 24 participants exceed 0.5 under the upper bound.

Individual variation is substantial and stable: the perparticipant range widens from 0.173 to 0.338 in BML12 and 0.120 to 0.297 in SG12 as the bound admits deferred reformulation, and 47 of 56 participants gain.
The gap distinguishes translators whose detection and action are tightly coupled from those who register problems later or register problems and defer acting.
There was no reliable association between sensitivity and accuracy.
9.7-18.4% (BML12) and 15.5-21.9% (SG12) of lower-bound type-2 = 1 events constitute potential self-repair leaks.
However, recoding them moves AUROC2 by at most 0.002.
A no-monitoring model suggests t = 0.69 for both groups under the upper bound.
These results largely mitigate the logical confound that would undermine an interpretation of AUROC2 due to the following assumptions: 1.
A semantically substantive drafting reformulation reflects a deliberate monitoring decision concerning the corresponding initial production.
Revision identifies and retains a suitably acceptable translation, such that the final translation provides the criterion against which the validity of the initial production can be evaluated 3.
When translators detect that an initial production is incorrect, they replace it with a correct formulation during drafting rather than deferring the correction to revision.
Over 90% of the between-participant variance in AUROC2 is driven by the P(reformulated | incorrect) group.
Despite this, the measure provides value over the use of the fraction of total corrections occurring during drafting for three reasons: 1.
The AUROC2 values can be situated within the broader set of metacognition literature.

Future metacognition studies on translation may use di"erent behavioural measures for trials, explicit confidence ratings, and externally assessed metrics for accuracy and this may change how much variance comes from P(reformulated | incorrect).
Future samples may exhibit very di"erent behaviour e.g. more reversions (which aren't captured by the fraction)

The Monitor Model (Tirkkonen-Condit 2005) describes translation as a two-part process: a default, low cost, largely automatic rendering procedure which renders the target text to closely mirror the source text's lexical and syntactic structure, and a supervisory monitor that intervenes when it has detected that a literal translation is inadequate, triggering an e"ortful strategic process.

In agreement with this notion, Tirkkonen-Condit et al. (2008) found that when typingerror revisions were excluded, 42.3% of revisions were corrections of literal translations. Carl and Dragsted (2012) further propose that comprehension and production occur as parallel processes rather than sequentially.

(2008)</ref> found that when typingerror revisions were excluded, 42.3% of revisions were corrections of literal translations. <ref type="bibr" target="#b11">Carl and Dragsted (2012)</ref> further propose that comprehension and production occur as parallel processes rather than sequentially.

text.text: This is consistent with their finding that long-distance revisions, show up as often during Drafting, as Revision because the monitor is active throughout production.
Continual monitoring during production also implies that error correction of a past production can occur at any point during the window in which monitoring is taking place.
How well a translator is able to notice that a previous action was incorrect is what is meant by metacognitive sensitivity.

This type of protracted metacognitive process di"ers from the standard visual discrimination tasks in several ways and crucially, error-detection may ensue through di"erent mechanisms: new source-text information provides additional evidence which allows the translator to retroactively reveal an earlier target-text span as incorrect.
This is evident through reformulation behaviour that occurs several PUs after the initial production (when additional context has concluded that an earlier literal translation was inadequate).
Post-decisional: a translator produces a span of text before 1 st order sensory evidence has fully accumulated.
Once this encoded sensory evidence reveals an inadequacy in the original production, a reformulation occurs.

Importantly, this type of sensory evidence accumulation is endogenous and has been found to decay faster over time than high-level task evidence, which conversely, benefits from additional time (Balsdon et al., 2024).
text.formatted: Importantly, this type of sensory evidence accumulation is endogenous and has been found to decay faster over time than high-level task evidence, which conversely, benefits from additional time <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">(Balsdon et al., 2024)</ref>.

text.text: These types of corrections may reflect more immediate corrections such as those contributing to the lower bound of the response window in this framework.
2 nd order evidence: the translator uses sensory information about the text as well as their experience during an initial production to decide whether they are confident about it or not.
For example, a translator may find a span of text di!
cult to translate and use the felt uncertainty at the time of production, as well as the text itself to form a confidence judgement.

Since this type of evidence does not rapidly decay over time (Balsdon et al., 2024), it is possible that such corrections guide the translator to return to a span of text much later in Drafting or the Revision phase.

text.text: This type of metarepresentation is not linguistic or pragmatic.
We cannot be sure whether any reformulation in the text was a result of either of the three cases outlined, and AUROC2 does not make a distinction.

Moreover, it is important to clarify the distinction between linguistic and cognitive metarepresentation: Compositional semantics builds increasingly complex representations but it may still be first-order content, regardless of its linguistically hierarchical structure.

According to Shreve (2009) and Angelone (2010), monitoring a text and controlling it through modifications and corrections, is a metacognitive skill central to translation expertise but this is not the same as metacognition under Fleming & Daw's (2017) definition who specifically refer to a representation whose content is another mental state.

text.text: The experimental design, di"ers from a standard visual metacognitive discrimination task in several structural ways and has several limitations: Proxy confidence measure: The current paradigm did not use explicit or implicit probes to measure confidence.
It used an implicit confidence proxy to preserve the underlying mechanism driving error-detection (Nicholson et al., 2019).
text.formatted: It used an implicit confidence proxy to preserve the underlying mechanism driving error-detection <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">(Nicholson et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Had explicit confidence probes been used to interrupt during Drafting, the underlying mechanism and AUROC2 may be di"erent.

The temporal decoupling of decision and response: In a typical visual task, the type-1 decision and the type-2 confidence judgment are yoked together, milliseconds to a couple of seconds apart, which limits the ways confidence-generating evidence accumulates.
The protracted response window used in this study introduces new sources of noise and evidence.
Dependence between trials and heterogeneity: In translation, segments of varying di!
culty are linked through discourse coherence and working memory.
SDT assumes trial-by-trial independence of the confidence/accuracy pairing.
Applying SDT to translation data stretches the model's assumption whenever cross-unit dependencies drive detection.
Memory dependence: the requirement of holding a span of text in memory adds an extra source of noise as signal decay is also a factor.
Signal distortion: Fleming and Dolan (2010) showed implicit measures are systematically distorted by factors unrelated to the underlying certainty signal (like loss aversion and wager size).
In translation, revising a span many words behind could cost more than fixing a recent error so translators may leave these cases for Revision even if they were detected during Drafting.
Binary confidence outcome: Studies tend to use 4-6 confidence bins to build a full ROC curve.
This study used a single operating point (2-bin) which mechanically compresses AUROC2 toward 0.5 relative to a graded bin design.
For these reasons, comparison to values from previous research provides limited value.

However, visual, retrospective, binary classification/detection tasks have produced AUROC2 in the range of 0.55-0.75 (Fleming et al., 2010; Mazor et al., 2020; Zizlsperger et al., 2016; Fleming et al., 2016; Sherman & Seth, 2024), typically clustering in the 0.6-0.7 range.

text.text: The present analysis would benefit from replication with a larger participant pool and the inclusion of a third language pair, which would allow language-general patterns to be distinguished from pair-specific artifacts.

It should also be acknowledged that the dataset analysed here was not originally designed to test the metacognitive questions raised in this study; it was assembled for other purposes within the CRITT TPR-DB, and a purpose-built study, with a controlled confidence-elicitation protocol and balanced item di!
culty, would allow more direct tests of claims.
A next step would be to apply the same tools used to ask how metacognitive sensitivity varies systematically with translator expertise and task di!
culty.
A further avenue is to extend Nicholson et al.'s (2019; 2021) dissociation between explicit and implicit uncertainty monitoring, and its link to mentalising ability, into the translation domain.
text.formatted: A further avenue is to extend <ref type="bibr" target="#b45">Nicholson et al.'s (2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr">2021)</ref> dissociation between explicit and implicit uncertainty monitoring, and its link to mentalising ability, into the translation domain.

text.text: Their work shows that explicit metacognitive judgments recruit the same resources as mentalising, while implicit uncertainty-monitoring tasks do not.
Translation is a strong test case for this dissociation, because Theory of Mind is integral to resolving ambiguity in a source text, tracking authorial intent, and rendering pragmatic nuance.

Moreover, using additional data could be useful: Incorporating additional implicit behavioral proxies for confidence, such as pause duration, typing rhythm, or gaze patterns would move the implicit measure from a single-point signal towards a graded confidence report, addressing the AUROC2-computability limitation discussed.
A di"erent question which could be asked is what the process of self-monitoring looks like as it unfolds in time.

A Drift Di"usion Model (DDM) or related evidence-accumulation model could be used to ask whether deferred reformulations show di"erent accumulation dynamics from reformulations made immediately upon production.

Specifically, one could test whether the proximate/deferred distinction is better explained by a di"erence in decision boundary (deferred reformulations could require more accumulated evidence before a revision is triggered) or by a di"erence in drift rate (deferred reformulations could reflect a slower-building signal), and whether the pause preceding a reformulation carries a measurable evidence-accumulation signature.
Such a project would constitute a substantial modelling undertaking and is proposed here as a direction for future research.
